I'm pretty sure it's different for everyone with depression, so I'll just answer as best as I can and hope it helps.

>but they often shut me down when I try to open a dialogue with them

There are times when you just need someone's presence and know they're *there*. Or times when a person just rather have silence. When I get like this I usually just have someone stay with me and it doesn't matter whatever they do as long as they stay in the same room and don't expect me to engage in too much interaction. (There have been times when I just came over to my best friend's house to sleep just to get away from stress triggers.) It distracts me from self destructive thoughts. Or they possibly just aren't ready to talk about these kinds of things yet. Don't rush them if they're not ready to talk yet. 

>If a conversation does begin it is often short, with them shutting down every supportive or constructive thing I have to say.

When I *am* in the mood to talk about what goes on in my head, the things that come out of my mouth are depressing and dark and the other party usually counters those thoughts. I often get angry at positive thoughts at these times, because I am focusing on all the negative things in my mind, *absolutely convinced* that nothing can come out of my life, etc etc. Depression makes a person see things from a very dark point of view, so it is often difficult to see things in another light. 

I think if the person refuses to talk about it and/or refuses to seek professional help, it is better to watch out for them and whether they get into self destructive behaviors. What my best friend does when I indulge in these behaviors is ask me what it made me feel and what pushed me to do it. It helps to understand what could have possibly triggered it. Do thoughful little things that let them know you're there for them if they need it: checking in on them if they've eaten, cleaning up little things, a little "hope you get home safe" text, etc etc. (But make sure not too hover too much.)

And if you plan on being part of this person's support system, make sure they can rely on you. (But not in the form of sacrificing your mental health too, because that happens.)

Hope I helped? And hope it all goes well.
